analysis.one_liner: Permanently dedicates offshore oil royalties to parks, land conservation, wildlife, and coastal restoration.
analysis.headline: The Resources 2000 Act, which would have guaranteed roughly $2 billion a year from offshore oil royalties for parks, land conservation, and wildlife, never got a vote in the House and died when Congress adjourned in January 2001.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would take money the federal government already receives from offshore oil and gas drilling and automatically put about $2 billion a year into parks, wildlife, and land protection instead of leaving it to annual budget fights. It would fund buying parkland and conservation land, fixing up federal parks and refuges, protecting farmland and ranchland from development, helping coastal states restore fisheries, paying states to protect native wildlife, and paying landowners to help endangered species recover. The money would be available every year without a separate vote of Congress.
analysis.who_benefits: Everyone who uses public lands, parks, and coastlines: the bill would have permanently guaranteed roughly $2 billion a year from existing offshore oil royalties for parkland acquisition, state and urban parks, farmland and forest protection, park and refuge repair, marine conservation, and wildlife protection — without raising taxes. Families in cities would gain nearby park investment; states and local governments would get matching grants; farmers and ranchers would be paid for permanent conservation easements; Indian tribes would get competitive restoration grants; and small landowners and family farms would get paid incentives to aid endangered species recovery.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Park users, coastal communities, and state wildlife programs

how_it_helps.text: Makes $900 million a year from the Land and Water Conservation Fund available automatically for federal land acquisition and state park grants, without requiring Congress to approve the money each year — money it had largely failed to appropriate, leaving an unallocated surplus of over $12 billion.

Directs $100 million a year to an Urban Park and Recreation Recovery Fund for matching grants to local governments to rehabilitate and develop neighborhood parks, aimed at cities whose park systems had been neglected for years.
Provides $150 million a year for historic preservation, with priority to endangered historic properties.
Creates a $150 million-a-year fund to buy conservation easements that keep farmland, ranchland, and forest from being developed, with the federal share limited to half the cost.

Dedicates $250 million a year to repairing and restoring degraded national parks, wildlife refuges, national forests, and Bureau of Land Management lands, including $25 million a year in competitive grants to Indian tribes.

Funds coastal-state marine conservation plans, state native fish and wildlife programs, and $100 million a year in incentives to private landowners to help recover endangered species, with priority for small landowners and family farms.

analysis.who_pays: No one pays through new taxes; the money comes from royalties already collected on offshore oil and gas drilling in the Gulf of Mexico that otherwise would have flowed to general federal accounts. In a narrow sense, other uses of that revenue — including deficit reduction or other federal programs — give up roughly $2 billion a year.
analysis.who_pays_short: Other claims on federal oil royalties

drawbacks.text: The bill's dedicated funding is tied to offshore oil and gas royalties, so conservation budgets would rise and fall with drilling activity and depend on continued offshore extraction rather than reducing it.
The land-protection programs pay landowners to permanently restrict farmland, ranchland, and forest from development, which can limit future tax bases and housing supply in fast-growing areas.
By making roughly $2 billion a year available without further appropriation, the bill permanently shifts spending decisions away from the annual congressional appropriations process.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits are large and broadly shared — permanent funding for parks, land protection, and wildlife, paid for from existing offshore oil royalties rather than new taxes or borrowing. The drawbacks are real but modest: funds are locked to offshore drilling revenue (a mild ongoing incentive for extraction), rural landowners receive payments for development restrictions that not everyone wants, and permanent appropriations reduce Congress's annual flexibility. On balance the public gain clearly outweighs the costs.

outcome.mechanism: The bill got a hearing in the House Natural Resources Committee but was never voted on or reported out, and it expired when the 106th Congress ended in January 2001.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on February 23, 1999, with 108 cosponsors, and referred to the House Natural Resources and Agriculture Committees.
The House Natural Resources Committee held hearings in March 1999, and parts were referred to subcommittees, but no markup or vote ever followed.
The bill received no further action after March 10, 1999, and died at the end of the 106th Congress without reaching the House or Senate floor.
The bill would have paid for conservation permanently from offshore oil and gas royalties, with money available each year without a separate vote.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Supporters of the funding status quo: the money stayed available for other uses, and no new conservation mandates or dedicated land-buying programs were created. Land developers also benefited from the absence of new open-space protection.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: The status quo: no dedicated conservation funding created

for.name: Rep. George Miller
for.role: Sponsor; senior House Natural Resources Committee member (D-CA)
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Resources 2000 Act and led its introduction.

for.name: 108 House cosponsors
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, including senior members and the House Democratic leader.

against.name: House Resources Committee leadership
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on the day it was introduced, held hearings, and never reported it out or scheduled a vote in the remaining 22 months of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: Support was overwhelmingly Democratic — 106 of 108 cosponsors were Democrats, with one Independent and one Republican — and the bill never advanced past hearings in a Republican-controlled House.

industries.industry: Land developers and suburban real estate interests
industries.note: The bill would fund permanent conservation easements and parkland acquisition that take land off the table for development, and its stated aim is to slow the loss of about 7,000 acres of farmland and open space a day.
Marine conservation funding would help rebuild fish populations and coastal ecosystems that fishing and coastal tourism depend on.
Better-funded parks, refuges, and coastal restoration support the trail, campground, and recreation infrastructure the outdoor economy relies on.

industries.industry: Ranchers, farmers, and family forest owners
industries.note: The bill pays willing landowners for permanent conservation easements worth up to half the value of their land, while keeping the land in productive use.

industries.industry: Oil and gas companies operating in the Gulf of Mexico
industries.note: The bill takes no new money from offshore drilling; it redirects royalties from existing Gulf of Mexico leases to conservation. It neither expands nor restricts drilling, but it entrenches a system in which conservation funding depends on continued extraction revenue.
The farmland, ranchland, and endangered-species programs route money through state agencies, tribes, and qualified nonprofit conservation organizations as matching-grant partners.
